sketches: The lamination conjecture together with the already-proved lower bound n(2,d) > (1−o(1))d²/2 yields lim n(2,d)/d² = 1/2 (as stated in the record); in particular the limit exists, answering the open question affirmatively.

source.name: n(2,d) asymptotic limit ½
source.statement: A general conjecture is posed in the final section which, together with the lower bound $n(2,d) > (1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$, would imply that $\lim_{d\to\infty} \frac{n(2,d)}{d^2} = \frac{1}{2}$.
source.context: The authors establish the lower bound $n(2,d) > (1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$, improving the previous bound $n(2,d) > \frac{d^2}{4}$. They remark that determining the precise asymptotic order of $n(2,d)$ seems to be a hard task (as noted earlier by Alon and by Huang–Sudakov), and refer to a formal conjecture in the final section concerning lamination-based constructions.

target.name: Existence of limit n(2,d)/d²
target.context: The authors conjecture that if the limit exists it equals $\frac{1}{2}$, but explicitly remark that even the existence of the limit is currently unknown. The paper provides the lower bound $n(2,d) > (1-o(1))\frac{d^2}{2}$ via Theorem 2.

sketches: If T(G) = Θ̃(√|G|) uniformly over all finite groups G, then T(p) = Θ̃(√p) for primes p (far below the current O(p^{3/4+ε}) upper bound, which relies on subgroups), and T(G) depends on the structure of G beyond its order only up to polylogarithmic factors — settling both parts of the question.

source.name: Minimal complement count T(n) square-root growth
source.statement: We have that $T(n) = \widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{n})$. More generally, we have that $T(G) = \widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{|G|})$.
source.context: The paper defines $\widetilde{\Theta}(g(n))$ to mean $f = \Omega(g(n)(\log n)^a)$ and $f(n) = O(g(n)(\log n)^b)$ for some integers $a,b$ (i.e., equality up to polylogarithmic factors). Theorem 1 gives a lower bound $T(n) \geq n^{1/3}/(2(\log n/\log 2)^{2/3})$ and Theorem 3 gives $T(n) = O(n^{3/4+\varepsilon})$; the conjecture proposes the true growth rate is $\widetilde{\Theta}(\sqrt{n})$.

target.name: T(p) upper bound for prime groups
target.statement: Is the behavior of $T(n)$ different when $n$ is prime? How much does $T(G)$ depend on the structure of $G$ in addition to the order of $G$?
target.context: The best upper bound constructions for $T(n)$ rely on the existence of subgroups of certain orders, so the best known upper bound for $T(p)$ when $p$ is prime is only $O(p^{3/4+\varepsilon})$, which may not be tight.

sketches: A closed Riemannian surface with cut locus (hence systole) bounded below by 1 and area at most α has genus bounded in terms of α by the systolic inequality for surfaces (area ≥ c·g/log²g when sys ≥ 1). So if the cop number of Riemannian surfaces is bounded by a function of the genus (positive answer to the first question), the supremum over the class in the second question is finite.

source.name: Cop number of Riemannian surfaces by genus
source.statement: Is the cop number of surfaces bounded in terms of the genus?
source.context: In Section 3 the author introduces a continuous Cops and Robbers game on Riemannian surfaces and poses several basic open questions. The first asks whether the cop number of a Riemannian surface, defined via players moving at unit velocity, is a finite function of the topological genus.

target.name: Cop number finiteness on bounded Riemannian surfaces
target.statement: What is the supremum of the cop numbers taken over all surfaces whose cut locus is at least $1$ and whose area is at most $\alpha$? Is it bounded?
target.context: The author asks whether restricting to Riemannian surfaces with a positive lower bound on the injectivity radius and an upper bound on total area is enough to guarantee a finite supremum for the cop number.

sketches: Jaeger showed that the k=2 case of his modular orientation conjecture (every 8-edge-connected graph has a modular 5-orientation) implies Tutte's 5-flow conjecture; the OPG page records this implication.
Jaeger showed the k=2 case (every 8-edge-connected graph has a modular 5-orientation, i.e. a 5/2-flow) implies that every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 5-flow; stated in the OPG entry.

source.name: Jaeger's modular orientation conjecture
source.statement: Conjecture Every $ 4k $ - edge-connected graph can be oriented so that $ {\mathit indegree}(v) - {\mathit outdegree}(v) \cong 0 $ (mod $ 2k+1 $ ) for every vertex $ v $ .
source.context: Jaeger called an orientation with the above property a modular $ (2k+1) $ - orientation , and observed that a graph has a modular $ (2k+1) $ -orientation if and only if it has a $ (2+\frac{1}{k}) $ -flow. Thus, this conjecture may be seen as a sharp form of the 2+epsilon flow conjecture . For k=1, this problem is precisely the 3-flow conjecture , and for k=2, Jaeger showed that this conjecture (if true) would imply the 5-flow conjecture . If true, this conjecture would be best possible for every value of k. The restriction of this conjecture to planar graphs is open, and has a dual formulation. See Mapping planar graphs to odd cycles .

target.name: 5-flow conjecture
target.statement: Conjecture Every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero 5-flow.
target.context: For planar graphs , this theorem follows from flow/coloring duality , and the Five color theorem (every loopless planar graph is 5-colorable). In light of this, we may view this conjecture as a widesweeping generalization of the 5-color-theorem. The Petersen graph does not have a nowhere-zero 4-flow, which shows that this conjecture (if true) is best possible. It is far from obvious that there should exist a fixed number $ k $ so that every bridgeless graph has a nowhere-zero $ k $ -flow. Indeed, this weaker conjecture was also made by Tutte, but was resolved by Kilpatrick [K] and independently Jaeger [J], who both proved that bridgeless graphs have nowhere-zero 8-flows. Seymour [S] improved upon this result by showing that bridgeless graphs have nowhere-zero 6-flows.
